title: Across 18,000 testable ribosome-translated ORFs in human UTRs and lncRNAs, 76,215 genomes show on average at most 6% of the amino-acid selection of canonical proteins of up to 150 amino acids
abstract:
On average, the peptides of short open reading frames (ORFs) that ribosomes translate in human 'non-coding' RNAs show very little sign that natural selection keeps their amino-acid sequence: at most about 6% of the selection in canonical proteins of up to 150 amino acids. This matters because thousands of these ORFs are now proposed as hidden protein-coding genes (microproteins), are added to the reference gene catalogue, and can be read as protein-changing in clinical work.

We tested the 28,531 ORFs of the GENCODE/TransCODE Ribo-seq catalogue (Ribo-seq: sequencing of RNA that ribosomes protect) in 5' leaders, 3' trailers, lncRNAs and processed transcripts with variants from 76,215 genomes (gnomAD v4.1); 18,053 ORFs had testable sites. Missense changes alter an amino acid; synonymous changes do not. Both alternate in the same codons, so their ratio cancels regional effects. Controls: the same ORFs read in the two shifted frames, and untranslated ATG ORFs in the same kinds of transcripts.

Missense observed/expected relative to synonymous was 0.80 (95% interval 0.78-0.82) in canonical proteins of up to 150 amino acids and 0.99-1.00 in untranslated ORFs. In Ribo-seq ORFs it was 0.986 (0.978-0.994), but frame +1 gave 0.983. The frame-specific depletion was 0.004 (-0.006 to 0.016) against 0.255: 1.7% of canonical selection, upper limit 6% (about 1,100 ORF-equivalents) and 11% relative to proteins of 100 amino acids or fewer; without the codons next to the start and stop codons it was 0.001 (-0.011 to 0.012). uORFs, lncRNA ORFs and ORFs with mass-spectrometry peptides were near zero; their start and stop codons were not more depleted than those of other upstream or lncRNA ATG ORFs, which can themselves be regulatory. Small signals in ORFs of 50 amino acids or fewer and in 581 ORFs with codon-like conservation in 241 mammals come in part from the codons next to the start and stop codons; without these codons they are not significant.

Limitations: the test detects selection of the strength of typical canonical proteins; canonical proteins of 50 amino acids or fewer and 46 annotated microprotein genes also gave no clear signal, so weak selection on real microproteins is not excluded, and single ORFs cannot be tested (about 2-15% power). We give per-ORF results and predictions for editing screens, larger cohorts and rare-disease studies.

display.caption: Missense depletion (left) and singleton excess (right) relative to synonymous sites in 76,215 genomes, in the annotated reading frame (blue) and two shifted frames (controls). Canonical proteins show strong frame-specific selection; Ribo-seq ORFs of every type are at the level of untranslated ATG ORFs. 95% gene-bootstrap intervals; non-CpG-transition sites.

Frame-specific amino-acid-level selection of Ribo-seq ORFs as a fraction of canonical proteins of up to 150 amino acids (0 = none, 1 = as in canonical proteins), by evidence class. No detectable association with peptide evidence. Phylo coding-like ORFs show some signal, but untranslated ATG ORFs chosen by the same rule (green) are not different.

Missense depletion and singleton excess against mammalian codon periodicity of phyloP (positions 1-2 minus 3). Canonical CDS (blue) rise with periodicity; Ribo-seq ORFs (orange) stay close to untranslated ATG ORFs (green).
